text: commanders with a full beard
notes: attribute: facial hair on the PRIMARY subject. The point of this query is the primary-vs-background split: a bearded villager behind the dragon must not count. Stubble and moustache-only faces are out; the slot value should read as a beard. Judged against the default printing.

text: commanders wearing a crown or circlet
notes: attribute: worn object on the head. Crowns, coronets and circlets count; helms, tiaras of horn, and antlers do not. Royal title in the card name is a strong prior but not the criterion - the crown has to be visible in the art.

text: commanders whose primary subject is a skeleton or a skull-faced undead figure
notes: attribute: exposed bone or a skull for a face on the primary subject. Fleshed zombies and hooded wraiths with no visible skull are out; this is the literal counterpart to the adversarial species queries.

text: commanders that are cat-headed humanoids
notes: attribute: species of the primary subject. Anthropomorphic cats standing upright, not four-legged big cats and not humans with a cat companion.

text: commanders that are merfolk with visible fins or a fish tail
notes: attribute: species of the primary subject, verified by fins, gills, or a tail rather than by the type line. Serpents, krakens and human sailors are out.

text: commanders that are angels with feathered wings
notes: attribute: feathered wings on a humanoid primary subject. Black feathers count; bat wings, insect wings and cloth banners mistaken for wings do not.

text: commanders that are dragons
notes: attribute: species of the primary subject. NOT exhaustive - the corpus holds well over a hundred legendary dragons, so this is a high-confidence sample and recall here is recall over a sample, not over the true gold set. Useful anyway: a retriever that misses half of THIS list is broken.

text: commanders holding a staff or walking stick rather than a weapon
notes: attribute: held object plus its is_weapon flag - the spec's 'holding something that isn't a weapon' case. Spears, scythes and bladed staves are excluded on purpose; the discrimination being tested is staff-vs-polearm, which is exactly where a merged description layer starts guessing.

text: commanders wearing a full-face helmet or mask that hides their features
notes: attribute: face occlusion. Open-faced helms and circlets are out; the face has to be genuinely unreadable. Tests whether the vision pass filled the clothing and pose slots instead of silently omitting them.

text: commanders standing in snow or on ice
notes: attribute: setting. Snowfall, drifts, glaciers or frozen water visible in the scene. A white or pale palette alone does not count - this separates setting from palette, which the slots keep apart.

text: commanders with fire or open flame in the picture
notes: attribute: an element present in the scene, whether held, worn, cast or burning in the background. Red mana symbols and warm palettes are not evidence.

text: commanders that are walking plants, treefolk, or fungus
notes: attribute: species of the primary subject - bark, leaves, vines or fungal caps forming the body itself. Druids standing in a forest are the near miss to reject.

text: commanders shown with a wolf or dog beside them
notes: attribute: a second figure of a specific species in the frame. Requires the other_figures slot to be populated rather than collapsed into the primary subject; cards where the canine IS the primary subject also count.

text: commanders that are goblins
notes: attribute: species of the primary subject. Paired with the adversarial dwarf-vs-gnome query: goblins are visually distinctive, so a miss here is a retrieval failure rather than a perception failure.

text: commanders with visible mechanical parts or a metal body
notes: attribute: body composition of the primary subject - plate, gears, etherium grafts, prosthetics. Characters merely holding an artifact are out.

text: commanders that look lonely
notes: register: affective. The spec's headline case. Should be reachable by BOTH routes: interpretive props that literally say isolated, and decomposition into single figure / empty landscape / cold palette against the literal layer. If only one route contributes, the blend is broken.

text: art that feels like the moment right before a betrayal
notes: register: narrative. Tests implied narrative and power dynamic between figures. Accept a result if two or more figures are present and the framing genuinely reads as tension about to break, not merely as combat already underway.

text: quietly menacing rather than overtly evil
notes: register: affective. The word 'rather' is doing real work - a result that is a screaming demon is WRONG even though it is evil. Precision here measures whether the router preserved the contrast instead of embedding the whole phrase.

text: would fit on a black metal album cover
notes: register: analogical. Expect monochrome forests, frost, silhouettes, corpse-pale figures. A merely dark fantasy scene in full colour is a near miss, not a hit.

text: feels like a Studio Ghibli character
notes: register: analogical. Warmth, roundness, quiet wonder, benign creature design. Tests whether interpretive props carry a stylistic analogy the vision model was never explicitly asked about.

text: looks like it belongs in a noir film
notes: register: analogical. Hard shadow, rain, low key light, a figure in a doorway. Mark accepted only when the lighting itself carries it, not when the card is merely black-aligned.

text: a single small figure against a huge empty background
notes: register: compositional. Pure geometry: figure_count 1 plus a dominant negative space. This is the compositional query most likely to be answered correctly by the decomposed route alone, so it is the control for A01.

text: painterly and muted, almost watercolour
notes: register: stylistic. Visible brushwork, soft edges, desaturated washes. Digital airbrush realism is the near miss.

text: looks like a woodcut or an engraving
notes: register: stylistic. Hatching, hard black line, limited or absent colour. Tests whether art_style was filled with something more useful than 'fantasy illustration'.

text: a figure seen from behind, walking away from the viewer
notes: register: compositional. Back turned, face not visible, motion away from frame. Included as an abstract rather than a literal query because a defensible exhaustive gold set cannot be enumerated by hand, not because it is subjective.

text: someone grieving, or standing over the dead
notes: register: affective/narrative. Distinguish mourning from menace: a necromancer raising corpses is a rejection even though the literal evidence overlaps almost exactly. Hard negative goldmine for Phase 12.

text: the aftermath of a battle rather than the battle itself
notes: register: narrative. Smoke, wreckage, stillness, a lone survivor. Any image of active combat is a rejection - this measures whether 'rather than' survived routing, like A03.

text: warm and domestic, somewhere you would want to sit down
notes: register: affective. Hearths, taverns, kitchens, gardens. Rare in the corpus by construction, so treat a low-yield pool as information about the corpus rather than a retrieval bug.

text: shot from below so the subject towers over the viewer
notes: register: compositional. Low camera angle, subject filling the upper frame, sky behind. Tests the composition slot specifically; if composition is mostly 'centered figure' across the corpus, this query will expose it.

text: would work as a 1970s prog rock gatefold sleeve
notes: register: analogical. Airbrushed cosmic vistas, impossible architecture, saturated skies, tiny figures for scale. The furthest-from-vocabulary analogy in the set and the best single probe of whether contrastive training helped.

text: art containing a readable inscription, rune, or written word
notes: failure: text in art. Vision models at art-crop resolution hallucinate plausible words on banners and tomes, or miss legible text entirely. Expect literal props asserting inscriptions that are not there, and near-zero correlation between the pool and the truth. Recorded to size the error, not to fix it.

text: commanders holding a scroll or banner whose writing can actually be read
notes: failure: text in art. Harder variant of X01: the model must distinguish 'writing is present' from 'writing is legible'. Expect it to conflate the two and return every scroll in the corpus.

text: art with exactly seven figures in it
notes: failure: counting past a handful. figure_count is reliable at 1-3 and guesswork above about 5. Expect the pool to be full of crowds of anywhere from four to twenty. If this ever scores well, suspect the gold set, not the model.

text: art showing more than twenty individual soldiers in an army
notes: failure: counting past a handful. Tests the boundary between counting and estimating. The correct behaviour is a description that says 'a large host', and the correct system behaviour is therefore recall via the phrase, not via the number. Watch whether the router tries to build a numeric slot filter.

text: art that depicts Urza
notes: failure: recognizing a specific named character. The vision pass is forbidden from seeing card names and is explicitly told not to name characters or infer lore, so no proposition can say 'Urza'. Expect the judge - which does know Magic lore - to confabulate matches from generic robed-artificer evidence. This is by design and the failure shape is what matters.

text: art that depicts Nicol Bolas
notes: failure: recognizing a specific named character. Same trap as X05 with an unusually distinctive silhouette (horned elder dragon), so it also measures how much lore leaks back in through the judge and the vision-verify step.

text: commanders that depict Gandalf
notes: failure: recognizing a specific named character. Third variant chosen because the character has many printings under different card names; the honest answer requires character identity the pipeline deliberately never records. Expect high-confidence wrong answers: any grey-bearded staff-carrying wizard.

text: commanders that are elves, not humans
notes: failure: distinguishing similar species. Pointed ears are often occluded by hair or a helmet, and the literal layer will frequently have written 'human'. Expect false positives on humans and false negatives on elves whose ears are hidden.

text: commanders that are dwarves and not gnomes, halflings, or short humans
notes: failure: distinguishing similar species. All four read as 'short bearded humanoid' at art-crop resolution. Overlaps L01 on purpose: a system that scores well on beards and badly here is behaving exactly as expected.

text: commanders that are true wolves, not werewolves or dogs
notes: failure: distinguishing similar species. Overlaps L13 on purpose. The literal layer records 'large canine'; the distinction the query asks for is often not visually determinable at all, which is the most useful negative result in this block.
